## Proof

Let the projections $P', Q', R'$ on the $x$-axis be equidistant with $|P'Q'| = |Q'R'| = s$. Writing the $x$-coordinates of $P, Q, R$ as $t,\; t+s,\; t+2s$ for some real $t$, the three points on $y = x^2$ are

$$P = (t,\, t^2),\quad Q = (t+s,\,(t+s)^2),\quad R = (t+2s,\,(t+2s)^2).$$

The area of $\triangle PQR$ is

$$\mathcal{A} = \tfrac12\bigl|\det(\overrightarrow{PQ},\,\overrightarrow{PR})\bigr|.$$

Compute the two edge vectors:

$$\overrightarrow{PQ} = Q - P = \bigl(s,\; (t+s)^2 - t^2\bigr) = \bigl(s,\; 2ts + s^2\bigr),$$

$$\overrightarrow{PR} = R - P = \bigl(2s,\; (t+2s)^2 - t^2\bigr) = \bigl(2s,\; 4ts + 4s^2\bigr).$$

The determinant is

$$\det = s\cdot(4ts + 4s^2) - (2s)\cdot(2ts + s^2) = 4ts^2 + 4s^3 - 4ts^2 - 2s^3 = 2s^3.$$

Therefore

$$\mathcal{A} = \tfrac12\,|2s^3| = s^3.$$

The result is independent of $t$, so the area is the same for every position of the equidistant triple along the parabola.

$$\boxed{\mathcal{A} = s^3}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
thinking:
The problem asks: On parabola y=x², three different points P, Q, R. Their projections on x-axis are equidistant with distance s. Find area of triangle PQR in terms of s.

Let me set up coordinates. Let the x-coordinates of P, Q, R be a-s, a, a+s (equidistant projections, distance s between consecutive). Actually the projections P', Q', R' on x-axis are equidistant with |P'Q'|=|Q'R'|=s. So x-coordinates are, say, x₀, x₀+s, x₀+2s. Let me set x₀ = t. So:
P = (t, t²), Q = (t+s, (t+s)²), R = (t+2s, (t+2s)²).

Area = (1/2)|det of [Q-P, R-P]|.
Q-P = (s, (t+s)²-t²) = (s, 2ts+s²)
R-P = (2s, (t+2s)²-t²) = (2s, 4ts+4s²)

det = s·(4ts+4s²) - 2s·(2ts+s²) = 4ts²+4s³ - 4ts²-2s³ = 2s³.

Area = (1/2)·|2s³| = s³.

So area = s³.

Let me verify: det = s(4ts+4s²) - 2s(2ts+s²) = 4ts²+4s³ - 4ts² - 2s³ = 2s³. Yes. Area = s³.

That's clean and independent of t. Good.
